what_it_does: Graph neural networks learn from data that comes as a network of connected nodes — social graphs, citation graphs, molecular graphs. Training them on large graphs across multiple GPUs is wasteful because the standard approach (data parallelism) samples the neighborhood of each target node independently on every GPU, causing the same nodes to be loaded and processed multiple times. GSplit fixes this by splitting each training batch into non-overlapping pieces, assigning each piece to exactly one GPU, and then having GPUs swap just the results they need from each other. This is up to 4.4x faster than the standard DGL library and up to 1.9x faster than the best prior caching-based system.
method_in_detail:
The idea. Graph neural networks work by aggregating information from a node's neighbors, then neighbors of neighbors, and so on for several hops. In the standard data-parallel approach, if you have 4 GPUs each processing a quarter of the target nodes, the same popular neighbor node often appears in all 4 GPUs' local subgraphs — so its features are loaded 4 times and its activations computed 4 times. On social networks, this redundancy can mean loading 2.5x as much data as necessary. GSplit (split parallelism) samples the full mini-batch once, then assigns each node in the sample to exactly one GPU. That GPU is solely responsible for loading and computing that node. GPUs then exchange needed intermediate results rather than raw input features.

How it works. The training iteration has three stages. During sampling, each GPU expands its assigned nodes outward to their neighbors layer by layer; when a neighbor belongs to a different GPU's partition, it is noted as a 'remote' node and a lightweight message is exchanged to claim it. This builds a 'shuffle index' — a compact lookup table of who needs what from whom. During loading, each GPU only fetches input features for the nodes in its own partition from CPU memory, with no redundant loads. During the forward pass through the neural network layers, each GPU computes the output of the nodes it owns, then sends those outputs (not raw features) to whichever GPU needs them for the next layer — one small all-to-all exchange per layer. The backward pass for computing gradients follows the same exchange pattern in reverse.

The key design choice — probabilistic offline splitting. The hardest part is deciding which nodes belong to which GPU. Doing this optimally for each sampled mini-batch at training time is computationally infeasible (it is an NP-hard graph partitioning problem). Instead, GSplit runs a one-time offline phase before training: it simulates many sample mini-batches, counts how often each node and each edge appears, assigns these as weights, and then runs the METIS graph partitioner on the weighted graph to find a global assignment that minimizes expected inter-GPU communication while balancing expected compute load. At training time each node is assigned to a GPU in constant time by a simple lookup.

The result. On three large real-world graphs (Orkut, Papers100M, Friendster) with GraphSAGE and GAT models, GSplit beats DGL by up to 4.4x (2.5x average), P3 push-pull parallelism by up to 4.1x, and the Quiver caching system by up to 1.9x, all with identical model accuracy.
